orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, continuing her story to Lockwood. It is Christmas, five weeks after Catherine was caught at Thrushcross Grange, so about December 1777. Near the end, after the asterisks, Lockwood interrupts and the two of them talk before Nelly goes on.

notes.g: Frances, Hindley's wife, now mistress of the Heights.

notes.t: there lighted from a handsome black pony
notes.g: There got down from a fine black pony.
notes.n: 'Light' (or 'alight') means to get down from a horse or carriage.

notes.g: A hat made of beaver-fur felt, trimmed with feathers.
notes.n: An expensive, fashionable riding hat.

notes.g: A riding habit: a woman's riding outfit with a long, full skirt.
notes.n: The skirt trailed so far that she had to hold it up to walk.

notes.g: Glide in grandly, like a ship.
Hindley's wife, now named by Nelly's story.
notes.n: Catherine's diary mentioned her in Chapter III.

notes.t: she must mind and not grow wild
notes.g: She must take care not to grow wild.

notes.n: 'Nelly' is a pet form of Ellen. The new mistress uses the more formal name.
'Frock' is the British word for a dress.

notes.g: Probably long white drawers showing below her skirt.
notes.n: Lace-trimmed drawers like these were a fashion for girls in Emily Brontë's own day.

notes.g: Jump up on her affectionately (as dogs do).
A rich, spiced fruit cake baked for Christmas.

notes.n: Not the old master and his wife, who have both died.
Literally 'clouded over', a joking, high-flown way to say dirty.

notes.g: Behind the settle: a long wooden bench with a high back, by the fire.

notes.t: fingers wonderfully whitened with doing nothing and staying indoors
notes.g: Pale hands, a sign of a lady who does no outdoor work.
notes.n: A tan or rough hands marked a working person. Ladies kept their skin white.
Pronounced 'BLAG-erd'.

notes.g: Hindley's jab: Heathcliff now ranks as a servant, not a member of the family.
Hindley, now master of the house.

notes.m: Then 'condescend' could be a compliment, meaning a superior kindly treating someone lower as an equal. Here Hindley is clearly being superior.

notes.g: A lady's personal maid, who helps her dress and does her hair.
Almost as bad as ordinary songs.
notes.n: To strict Joseph, only hymns and psalms are fit to sing. Worldly 'songs' are sinful, and cheerful carols come close.

notes.m: 'Gay' meant bright and cheerful. 'Sundry' means various; 'trifles' are small, cheap things.

notes.g: Her beloved children, Edgar and Isabella.
Spices warming for the Christmas drinks and baking.
Decorated with holly, a Christmas custom.
Beer heated with sugar and spices, a Christmas drink.

notes.t: the speckless purity of my particular care
notes.g: The spotless cleanness of the thing I took special pride in.
Catherine and Hindley's dead father, the old master.

notes.n: In northern dialect 'cant' means lively or cheerful. Not the preachy 'cant' of Chapter VI.

notes.g: A silver coin worth twelve pence, a twentieth of a pound.
notes.n: A generous gift for a servant girl.

notes.g: A Christmas tip or present given to servants.
notes.n: The origin of 'Boxing Day', the day after Christmas, in Britain.

notes.g: Put right some of the wrongs done to him.
The yard in front of the house.

notes.n: To 'don' is to put on clothes (from 'do on').
A joke on the country custom of leaving food out for the fairies.
'Dour' is a northern and Scottish word for stern and gloomy. 'Dumb' means silent, not stupid.

notes.t: a world of things to order

notes.g: Going without food and thinking things over.
notes.n: Nelly's slightly joking religious phrase: fasting and reflection were how Christians did penance.

notes.t: Proud people breed sad sorrows for themselves
notes.g: Proud people bring trouble on themselves.
notes.n: Nelly likes to speak in proverbs.

notes.t: I wish I had light hair and a fair skin
notes.g: Heathcliff wishes he looked like Edgar.
notes.n: Fair looks were linked with gentility then, and Heathcliff has been insulted for his darkness since he arrived.

notes.m: Not a drinking glass. 'Looking-glass' was the usual word for a mirror.

notes.n: Pronounced like 'dessert', as in 'just deserts'.

notes.m: 'Regular' here means thorough, out-and-out, not ordinary.
notes.n: Nelly's words reflect the prejudice of her time, but her point is that a good heart matters more than looks.

notes.g: Like the hidden prince of a fairy tale.

notes.t: Emperor of China, and your mother an Indian queen
notes.g: Nelly invents royal parents for him.
notes.n: To the English of the time, China and India stood for fabulous, exotic wealth. It is a kind fantasy. His real origins are unknown.
Mr. Earnshaw found him in Liverpool, a great port full of sailors (Chapter IV).

notes.t: frame high notions of my birth
notes.g: Imagine that I came from a noble family.

notes.t: the oppressions of a little farmer
notes.g: The bullying of a mere small farmer (Hindley).
notes.n: Nelly cuts Hindley down to size: he is only a modest country landowner.

notes.g: The Lintons ride in their own carriage, a sign of greater wealth.
notes.n: The Earnshaws ride to church on horseback.

notes.g: As bad luck would have it.
A small attic room right under the roof.

notes.n: A coxcomb is a vain, showy man, named after the jester's cap shaped like a rooster's comb.
'Master' was the polite title for a young boy of good family.

notes.g: The long neck hair of a young horse.

notes.n: Nelly notes that Heathcliff already saw Edgar that way.

notes.t: a tureen of hot apple sauce
notes.g: A deep serving bowl of hot apple sauce.
notes.n: Apple sauce was the usual partner for roast goose.

notes.g: A handkerchief of fine white linen, a sign of a rich child.

notes.t: That brute of a lad has warmed me nicely
notes.g: That brute of a boy has made me hot (from beating him).

notes.t: take the law into your own fists
notes.n: A twist on the saying 'take the law into your own hands'.

notes.g: Roast goose was the traditional English Christmas dinner then.
notes.n: Turkey became the usual Christmas bird much later.
In Catholic belief, purgatory is a place of suffering where souls are cleansed before entering heaven.
In northern speech, to 'weary for' something is to long for it.
'Mess' meant a portion of food. 'Victuals' is pronounced 'vittles'.

notes.g: Fill the gap (by being Isabella's partner).

notes.t: the Gimmerton band, mustering fifteen strong
notes.g: The village band from Gimmerton, fifteen players and singers.
notes.n: Village bands toured the better houses at Christmas, playing for money, food and drink.

notes.g: A large stringed instrument like a cello, common in village bands.
The homes of the better-off families.
Songs for several voices, often unaccompanied, popular in the 1700s.
The devil's hymn-singing: Joseph's name for the carols.
notes.n: 'Psalmody' is the singing of psalms. Joseph thinks the merry music is wicked.

notes.t: It is for God to punish wicked people
notes.g: Revenge belongs to God, not to us.
notes.n: Nelly echoes the Bible: 'Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord' (Romans 12:19).

notes.m: 'Divert' here means amuse, not turn aside.

notes.g: Thin, runny porridge, given to sick people.
notes.n: Lockwood is still recovering from his cold (Chapter IV).

notes.g: Probably the late hours, when the clock strikes eleven and twelve.
Stays in bed until ten in the morning.

notes.t: the very prime of the morning
notes.g: The best part of the morning.
A stubborn cold that won't go away.

notes.t: put you seriously out of temper
a spider in a dungeon does over a spider in a cottage
notes.g: A prisoner values a spider more than a cottager does.
notes.n: In a dungeon a spider may be the only company, so it seems fascinating. Lockwood means country people seem more interesting because there is less to distract you.

notes.t: I could fancy a love for life here almost possible
notes.g: I could almost imagine a lifelong love being possible here.

notes.t: a fixed unbeliever in any love of a year’s standing
notes.g: Lockwood didn't believe any love could last even a year.
notes.n: Remember his seaside romance in Chapter I, which he ran away from.

notes.g: Grand houses hired French chefs, who served many dishes at once.

notes.t: a mere atom in his regard
notes.g: A tiny part of his attention.

notes.t: a striking evidence against that assertion
notes.g: A clear proof against that claim.
Typical of people of your social class (servants).
notes.m: 'Peculiar' here means belonging to, not strange.

notes.n: 'Body' meaning a person is still heard in northern England and Scotland.

notes.g: The book room here at Thrushcross Grange.
Nelly's humble background: she couldn't be expected to read foreign languages.
notes.n: Greek and Latin were taught to gentlemen's sons, not to servants or to most girls.
Lockwood hoped in Chapter IV that she would be 'a regular gossip'.

notes.t: the summer of 1778, that is nearly twenty-three years ago
notes.g: So Lockwood is hearing this late in 1801.
notes.n: Chapter I opened with the date 1801.
